name: ESP8266EX
title: ESP8266EX: 2.4 GHz 802.11 b/g/n Wi-Fi system-on-chip with a 32-bit Tensilica L106 core, QFN32 5 × 5 mm
summary: A single-chip Wi-Fi controller: an 802.11 b/g/n (HT20) radio with its own power amplifier, low-noise amplifier, balun and antenna switch, a Tensilica L106 32-bit processor running up to 160 MHz, on-chip SRAM and ROM, and digital peripherals (GPIO, UART, SPI, HSPI, SDIO slave, I2C, I2S, PWM, IR, a 10-bit ADC). User code lives in an external SPI flash of up to 16 MB. It runs from 2.5 to 3.6 V, from -40 to 125 °C, and can either run the application itself or serve a host processor as its Wi-Fi interface over SPI, SDIO or UART. Its status is NRND (not recommended for new designs); Espressif names the ESP8684 as its successor.
key_figures: -98 dBm DSSS 1 Mbps; -72 dBm HT20 MCS7

tables.title: Power consumption by power mode
rows: Wi-Fi TX packet; Wi-Fi RX packet
notes: Modem-sleep: the CPU keeps running (for PWM or I2S work, say) while the Wi-Fi modem is switched off between beacons under 802.11 power save (U-APSD), holding the connection. At DTIM3, sleeping 300 ms and waking 3 ms for each beacon, the draw is about 15 mA.
Light-sleep: as modem-sleep, but the CPU is suspended too. At DTIM3 with the same 300 ms sleep and 3 ms wake, the draw is about 0.9 mA.
Deep-sleep: Wi-Fi is off and only the RTC runs. The 20 μA figure is taken at 2.5 V. A sensor that measures every 100 s, sleeps 300 s and then joins the AP (0.3 ~ 1 s) averages under 1 mA overall.

operation.text: The chip either runs the whole application itself, booting from its SPI flash, or acts as a Wi-Fi adapter for another microcontroller, attached over SPI, SDIO or UART. Antenna switch, balun, PA, LNA, filters and power management are on the die, so few outside parts are needed.

802.11 b/g/n, with 802.11n at 2.4 GHz up to 72.2 Mbps (MCS0-7, 20 MHz channels, 0.4 μs short guard interval, 2 x 1 STBC receive). Two virtual Wi-Fi interfaces; station, SoftAP and promiscuous modes in an infrastructure BSS; defragmentation; hardware TSF for automatic beacon monitoring; RTS/CTS and immediate block ACK; CCMP, TKIP, WEP and CRC done in the MAC; Bluetooth coexistence for single or dual antenna, optionally receiving Wi-Fi and Bluetooth at once. Transmit power reaches 20.5 dBm and can be adjusted.

The receiver mixes the RF down to I/Q baseband and converts it with two fast ADCs, with RF and baseband filtering, AGC and DC-offset removal on chip. The transmitter mixes I/Q up to 2.4 GHz and feeds the antenna through a CMOS PA linearised by digital calibration: +19.5 dBm average for 802.11b and +18 dBm for 802.11n MCS0. Carrier leakage, I/Q phase mismatch and baseband nonlinearity are calibrated out internally. The 2.4 GHz quadrature synthesizer is fully integrated, inductors, varactors, loop filter, regulators and dividers included, and self-calibrates.

Tensilica L106 32-bit RISC core, maximum clock 160 MHz. With the RTOS and the Wi-Fi stack running, about 80% of its capacity is left for the application. It reaches memory over an instruction bus (iBus, which can also fetch from flash), a data bus (dBus) and an AHB bus for registers; an arbiter serves requests in the order they arrive.

On-chip SRAM and ROM; none of the ROM is programmable, so user code is kept in external SPI flash, up to 16 MB in principle. Flash needed: at least 512 kB with OTA off, at least 1 MB with OTA on. Standard, dual and quad SPI flash modes are supported, and the image must be flashed in the mode the flash part uses. With the current SDK, in station mode joined to a router, heap plus data space left to the user is about 50 kB.

The RF mixers run from a high-frequency clock taken from the on-chip oscillator and an outside crystal of 24 MHz to 52 MHz; internal calibration lets many different crystals work, though crystal quality still affects phase noise and sensitivity. An external clock of 24 MHz to 52 MHz may be fed in instead, 0.8 Vpp to 1.5 Vpp.

Active: radio on, transmitting, receiving or listening. Modem-sleep: CPU running, Wi-Fi and radio off. Light-sleep: CPU and all peripherals paused; a MAC, host, RTC timer or external interrupt event wakes the chip. Deep-sleep: only the RTC is powered. For wake from deep-sleep, XPD_DCDC (GPIO16) is wired to EXT_RSTB.
VDD33 should rise within 10 μs to 2000 μs. EXT_RSTB follows at least 0.1 ms after VDD33 is up and CHIP_EN at least 0.1 ms after EXT_RSTB is high, each edge rising within 2 ms.
GPIO0, GPIO2 and MTDO are sampled at start-up to choose the boot mode and the SDIO mode. U0TXD must not be pulled low externally during power-up.

17 GPIOs, each assignable by register to other functions (I2C, I2S, UART, PWM, IR and more). Every pad has a tristate output and an input buffer, non-inverting, and can be set to high impedance. Pull options: XPD_DCDC has an internal pull-down only; every other GPIO pad has an internal pull-up only. Inputs land in registers and can raise CPU interrupts on an edge or a level.
One SDIO slave: SDIO v1.1 at 25 MHz and v2.0 at 50 MHz, in 1-bit and 4-bit SD modes and SPI mode.
Two SPI ports, the general SPI and HSPI, each able to be master or slave, with their pins in hardware. General SPI clocks to 80 MHz as master and 20 MHz as slave; HSPI clocks to 20 MHz.
One I2S input and one I2S output, served by linked-list DMA, for audio and other serial data streams; WS2812 LED strings can be driven from it.

At power-on UART0 sends boot messages at a rate set by the crystal: 115200 baud with a 40 MHz crystal, 74880 baud with 26 MHz. Where that output upsets the attached device, UART0 can be swapped from (U0TXD, U0RXD) to (MTDO, MTCK) for the power-on period.

Four PWM outputs, done in software and extendable by the user. In the LED smart-light demo a timer interrupt generates them, with resolution down to 44 ns; the period is settable from 1000 μs to 10000 μs (1 kHz to 100 Hz). At 1 kHz the duty step is 1/22727, better than 14 bits.

One infrared port, done in software, with NEC coding, modulation and demodulation. Carrier 38 kHz at 1/3 duty. Range is about 1 m, set by the pin's maximum drive current and the current-limiting resistance at the receiver: more resistance, less current and less power.

10-bit SAR ADC on TOUT (pin 6). It measures either the VDD3P3 supply, with TOUT floating, or an outside voltage of 0 to 1.0 V on TOUT, not both; vdd33_const in the RF initialization data and the software call change with the choice.
